informationChunks.wilmaIntro: Hi! I'm Wilma, your guide in this game. You're about to explore DATA VISUALIZATIONS – ones that show how data changes over time.
informationChunks.wilmaIntro2: We'll go through three types of visualizations. First, you’ll learn how they work. Then you’ll solve tasks, earn points, and move to the next level!
informationChunks.scoringSystem: Each correct answer earns 50 points. Each wrong one loses 25.
informationChunks.badges: Earn as many points as you can to unlock the <color=#FECA47>GOLD badge</color> in each level. Get gold in all, and you’ll earn the <color=#FECA47>MASTER badge</color> – only for true pros!
informationChunks.chartIntro: You’ll learn how to read line charts, area charts, and stream graphs. We’ll start with the easiest – the <color=#639C4E>LINE CHART</color>. You might already know it!
informationChunks.chartDefinition: Line charts show how a <color=#639C4E>value changes over time</color>, using <color=#639C4E>connected data points</color>.
informationChunks.axes: Every chart has two AXES – one horizontal, one vertical – that form the base.
informationChunks.xAxis: The X-AXIS runs horizontally and usually shows time. Here, it shows days in March.
informationChunks.yAxis: The Y-AXIS runs vertically and shows values, like temperature in °C.
informationChunks.dataPoints: The DOTS are data POINTS. Each shows a value at a specific time. Like: 10°C on 1.3.
informationChunks.line: The LINE connects the dots and shows TRENDS – when values rise or fall over time.
informationChunks.example: For example, it got colder from March 14 to March 21.
informationChunks.peeksTroughs: PEAKS are high points before a drop. TROUGHS are low points before a rise. The highest and lowest are called EXTREMES.
informationChunks.extremes: The highest value is the <color=#639C4E>MAXIMUM</color>. The lowest is the <color=#639C4E>MINIMUM</color>.
informationChunks.uses: Line charts are used in real life – to show stock prices, track business growth, or monitor health data like heart rate.

informationChunks.axesIntro1: Lets look at another example, which shows how CO2 emissions per person in Europe have changed over time. CO2 emissions happen when carbon dioxide (CO2) is released into the air, for example, when fuel is burned in the engine of a car.
informationChunks.axesIntro: We will start with axes. Our graph has two axes, the horizontal x-axis and vertical y-axis. Values on the x-axis represent dates (years) and values on the y-axis represent tons of CO2 per capita.
informationChunks.axesAssignment: Can you help me label these axes in the graph? Drag the labels from the right panel to the graph.

informationChunks.findTrendIntro: Next, let’s look at trends – times when values went up or down for several days in a row.
informationChunks.findTrendUpAssignment: Can you connect the points where CO2 levels are going only up over time?
informationChunks.findTrendDownAssignment: Great! Now do the same for periods where CO2 levels are going only down.

informationChunks.multilineintro1: A line chart can have multiple lines, which lets us compare different developments.
informationChunks.multilineintro2: For example, we can show not only <color=#35A8B7>Europe’s</color> CO2 emissions, but also those of other <color=#639C4E>world regions</color>.
informationChunks.multilineintro22: This works because all regions use the same kind of data: <color=#639C4E>dates</color> on the x-axis and <color=#639C4E>CO2 emissions per person</color> on the y-axis.
informationChunks.multilineintro3: Each region’s data points are plotted in the chart and shown in <color=#639C4E>different colors</color> to tell them apart.
informationChunks.multilineintro4: Then, points of the <color=#639C4E>same color</color> are <color=#639C4E>connected with a line</color>. Tap buttons to reveal other regions.
informationChunks.multilineintro5: Now you can compare! <color=#406A77>Australia</color>, <color=#CBEDB2>North America</color>, and <color=#35A8B7>Europe</color> emit more CO2 per person than <color=#FFD35C>Asia</color>, <color=#FE9748>South America</color>, and <color=#D43535>Africa</color>.
informationChunks.multilineintro6: You can also spot GLOBAL TRENDS in emissions at a glance.

informationChunks.chartIntro: Next up: AREA CHARTS! They're like line charts but with a filled area that shows size or volume along with the trend.
informationChunks.keyComponents: Area charts have the same basics — <color=#639C4E>axes, data points, and a line</color>. The x-axis usually shows <color=#639C4E>time</color>, the y-axis shows <color=#639C4E>value</color>.
informationChunks.keyComponents2: But here, the filled area matters most — points might not be marked.
informationChunks.areaReveal: Want to see the filled area? Try dragging left to right across the chart!
informationChunks.areaExplanation: This chart shows <color=#639C4E>total rainfall</color> during a month. It only goes up because <color=#639C4E>totals can’t go down</color>. Check the right panel for details.
informationChunks.visibleInfo: Area charts show <color=#639C4E>totals over time</color>, not just <color=#639C4E>trends</color>. Steep areas = more rain. Flat = little or none.
informationChunks.uses: They’re great for showing things that add up over time — like rainfall, pollution, sales, or web traffic.

informationChunks.activityIntro: Let’s see how area charts can be used to <color=#639C4E>compare data</color>. Below are two charts showing monthly rainfall in 2023.
informationChunks.activityIntro2: The left shows <color=#639C4E>Innsbruck, Austria</color> (moderate climate), the right shows <color=#639C4E>Tutunendo, Colombia</color> (tropical rainforest). Take a moment to look at both.
informationChunks.linkedAxes: At first, they may look similar — but check the y-axes. They use different scales. Click the button on the right to link the scales and see the real difference. You can switch between views anytime.
informationChunks.scalesInfo: The <color=#639C4E>y-axis scale</color> affects how we read data. A high max (like 1500 mm for Innsbruck) would flatten the chart and hide trends.
informationChunks.scalesInfo2: But when comparing two charts, using different scales can be misleading. They may look similar, even if the real values are very different.
informationChunks.questionsIntro: Now let’s explore what the charts tell us. Tap the answers in the right panel to respond to the questions!

informationChunks.chartIntro: The area chart you saw before was based on a line chart. Now let’s explore the STACKED AREA CHART — it also has multiple lines, showing multiple categories together.
informationChunks.reminder: Reminder: We can compare multiple categories in one chart because they use the <color=#639C4E>same type of data</color> — years on the x-axis, CO2 per year on the y-axis.
informationChunks.remind: We use a <color=#639C4E>legend</color> to label each colored area: <color=#406A77>gas</color>, <color=#FFD35C>oil</color>, and <color=#D43535>coal</color>. The buttons with names and colors help you toggle them.
informationChunks.linesIntro: A line chart can show how much CO2 came from coal in 1960. But what if we want to see the total CO2 from coal, gas, and oil?
informationChunks.linesIntro2: We could add them manually — but the stacked area chart does it for us! Click the stack button in the top right to see it happen.
informationChunks.stackingMotivation: In a stacked area chart, values are <color=#639C4E>stacked</color> on top of each other. That means we <color=#639C4E>add up</color> the values for each year from all categories.
informationChunks.stackingExample: For example, in 1960: gas = 4, oil = 9, coal = 17 → total = 30. Each point on the top line shows the sum.
informationChunks.cumulatingIntro: Want to compare just <color=#D43535>coal</color> and <color=#406A77>gas</color>? Just click the '<color=#FFD35C>oil</color>' button to hide it. You can turn categories on or off anytime.
informationChunks.cumulatingValuesUses: Use the 'stack' and 'unstack' buttons to switch between chart types. Use category buttons to control what’s shown.
informationChunks.cumulatedAreasControl: Stacked area charts show <color=#639C4E>trends and totals</color>, and also <color=#639C4E>how each category contributes</color> to the full value.
informationChunks.summary: They let us see the big picture and compare parts of the data — all in one view.

informationChunks.activityIntro: Awesome! Now that you know stacked area charts, let’s test your skills. You can use some tools: <color=#639C4E>click a category</color> to highlight it. Click again to return to the full view.
informationChunks.visualizerWindow: See the window on the right? Click or drag on the chart to check the selected category’s value. This <color=#639C4E>window</color> shows the <color=#639C4E>individual value</color> for that category (not the ones below it). To see the <color=#639C4E>total</color>, check the <color=#639C4E>y-axis</color>. Use both to help answer the next questions.

informationChunks.chartIntro: Last stop: the STREAM GRAPH! It’s based on the stacked area chart, but with a unique twist.
informationChunks.dataIntro: Below is a stacked area chart showing CO2 emissions per person across world regions (1950–2022) — similar to what you saw earlier.
informationChunks.dataIntro2: Click the centering button to turn it into a stream graph.
informationChunks.nameExplanation: See how the chart flows around the center like a river? The categories look like streams moving through time — that’s why it’s called a stream graph or theme river.
informationChunks.streamIntro: It shows the same data, but here the <color=#639C4E>Y-axis isn't as important</color>. Values are <color=#639C4E>stacked symmetrically</color> to create a smooth, centered flow.
informationChunks.streamIntro2: Stream graphs are best for showing <color=#639C4E>proportions</color> over time — not exact totals.
informationChunks.usesAbstract: They're great for spotting trends and changes in share, like which region’s emissions grew or shrank. But for totals, a stacked area chart is more accurate.
informationChunks.usesPractice: You’ll see stream graphs in economics, entertainment, sports, or climate science. The symmetrical layout looks balanced — but it’s created by a computer algorithm, since doing it by hand would be nearly impossible!

informationChunks.chartIntro: Explore each region and see how much it contributes to total emissions. <color=#639C4E>Click a category</color> to highlight it, and click again to remove the highlight. Drag across the chart to track changes over time — the top right panel shows the values.
informationChunks.exploreControls: When you're done exploring, click to move on to the next page.

informationChunks.chartIntro: Here’s another stream graph example — this time showing the <color=#639C4E>causes of deforestation</color> in the Amazon. The time span is short, so the data has fewer points. That’s why the streams look jagged when centered. Try turning on curves to smooth it out.
informationChunks.categorySizes: Not all categories are the same size. <color=#639C4E>Pasture use</color> dominates here, making smaller causes harder to see. Click the category labels on the right to hide large segments and focus on the smaller ones.

informationChunks.exploreControls: Same as the last time, you can click or drag across categories to highlight them and see their precise contributions in the right panel.

informationChunks.chartIntro: Explore how each region contributes to <color=#639C4E>CO2 emissions per person</color>. <color=#639C4E>Click a category</color> to highlight it, and click again to remove it. Drag across the chart to track changes — the top right panel shows the values over time.
